lesson_title: Snap the Branch: How Earthquakes Really Work
hook_text: Two earthquakes, same year. One was 500 times more powerful — and killed far fewer people. Why?
clip_script: Take a dry branch about as thick as your thumb and start bending it over your knee. Nothing happens at first — except that it is happening: the branch is loading up with your effort, storing it, pressing back harder and harder. Keep going. Then CRACK — the branch gives way, both halves spring violently straight, and the snap stings your palms. You have just run a complete earthquake. The push of the plates is your hands. The locked fault is the wood holding on. The years of quiet are the long slow bend — nothing visible, everything loading. The snap is the fault slipping, and the sting in your palms is the stored energy arriving at the surface as shaking. The rock does not explode; it springs back. And here is the part that decides who survives: earthquakes do not kill people — buildings do. In 2010, Chile's earthquake released around five hundred times the energy of Haiti's, yet Haiti buried hundreds of times more people. One country builds, inspects and drills. The other could not. Same planet, same physics, different vulnerability.
visual_style: Slow-motion branch bending and snapping intercut with a fault cross-section loading and lurching; split-screen Chile-Haiti skylines, one swaying and standing, one falling.
mood: Hands-on physics turning sober — a snap you can feel, a lesson that saves lives.
pacing: Tension building through the bend, explosive at the crack, measured and serious on the Chile-Haiti comparison.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to learn the triangulation trick that finds any epicentre.
